mainTopic: How the words of a נדר are understood: seafarers, 'those who see the sun,' 'the black-headed ones,' and ילודים and נולדים
overview: The גמרא finishes explaining who counts as יורדי הים (seafarers) and who counts as יושבי היבשה (land-dwellers). In a second version, everyone counts as a land-dweller, because even sailors come back to land. Next comes a series of new משניות about the words people use in a נדר. A vow from 'those who see the sun' includes the blind, because it covers everyone the sun shines on. A vow from 'the black-headed ones' includes bald and gray-haired men but not women or children, because the name belongs to men. A vow from ילודים does not include נולדים, but a vow from נולדים includes ילודים. רבי מאיר disagrees, and the גמרא explains his opinion by saying the משנה is missing words. רב פפא and אביי then show from פסוקים that נולדים can mean either 'already born' or 'will be born,' so for vows we follow everyday speech. Finally, the חכמים's phrase 'whose nature is to be born' leaves out fish and birds.

steps.title: Seafarers means real sailors, not short coastal travelers
steps.stepSummary: In the first version, the גמרא explains the רישא. People who travel from עכו to יפו count as land-dwellers, so 'seafarers' means people who regularly sail out to sea.
steps.simpleTranslation: Not those who travel from Akko to Jaffa, since these are land-dwellers. Rather, it means those whose way is to set sail.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes its first reading of the רישא of the משנה: 'one who vows from seafarers is permitted with land-dwellers.' It defines who counts as a 'seafarer.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: A short trip along the coast from עכו to יפו does not make someone a seafarer, so those travelers stay on the 'land-dweller' side. 'Seafarers' means people who regularly head out to sea. So the vow forbids only real sailors, and the coastal travelers stay permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: those who dwell on dry land
seafarers, literally 'those who go down to the sea'
to set sail, to head out to sea
from עכו to יפו, a short trip along the coast

phrases.english: [not] those who travel from Akko to Jaffa,
phrases.notes: This sentence started on the previous page. There the גמרא is explaining what 'seafarers' means in the first case of the משנה.

phrases.english: for these are land-dwellers,
rather, [it means] from those whose way is to set sail.

steps.triggerLanguage: הַהוֹלְכִים מֵעַכּוֹ לְיָפוֹ, דְּהָלֵין יוֹשְׁבֵי הַיַּבָּשָׁה נִינְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the first version, which reads the explanation on the רישא and began on the previous page.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In a vow from seafarers, coastal travelers count as land-dwellers. Only people who regularly sail out to sea are forbidden.

steps.title: Second version: even real sailors count as land-dwellers
steps.stepSummary: Another version reads the explanation on the סיפא. Someone who vows from land-dwellers is forbidden even from real sailors, because every sailor eventually comes back to land.
steps.simpleTranslation: The one who teaches it on the latter clause teaches it this way: One who vows from those who dwell on dry land is forbidden with seafarers. This applies not only to those who travel from Akko to Jaffa, but even to one who regularly sets sail, since in the end he comes up onto dry land.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second way of learning the same explanation, this time on the סיפא of the משנה: 'one who vows from land-dwellers is forbidden with seafarers.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the question is how wide 'land-dwellers' reaches. Coastal travelers are clearly included. Even someone who regularly sails is included too, because nobody stays at sea forever. Everyone ends up back on land, so everyone counts as a land-dweller.

keyTerms.meaning: the one who teaches it, meaning another version of the teaching
the latter clause of the משנה

steps.confusionAlert: Both versions agree that people traveling from עכו to יפו are land-dwellers. The difference is that the first version is about the vow from seafarers, and this one is about the vow from land-dwellers. Here even regular sailors are counted as land-dwellers.

phrases.english: And the one who teaches it on the latter clause
teaches it this way:
One who vows [not to benefit] from those who dwell on dry land
is forbidden with seafarers,

phrases.aramaic: וְלֹא בְּאֵלּוּ הַהוֹלְכִים מֵעַכּוֹ לְיָפוֹ בִּלְבַד,
phrases.english: and not only with those who travel from Akko to Jaffa,
but even with one whose way is to set sail,
since in the end he comes up onto dry land.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second version that attaches the explanation to the סיפא instead of the רישא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A vow from land-dwellers forbids even people who regularly sail, since everyone eventually returns to land.
steps.whatToRemember: In a נדר, we figure out who is included by how people normally use the words. 'Land-dwellers' can include everyone, because everyone ends up on land.

steps.title: New משנה: a vow from those who see the sun includes the blind
steps.stepSummary: Someone who vows from 'those who see the sun' is forbidden even from blind people. His words refer to everyone the sun shines on.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: One who vows from those who see the sun is forbidden even with the blind, because he meant only those whom the sun sees.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה gives another case of reading the words of a vow: 'those who see the sun.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: One might think 'those who see the sun' leaves out blind people, since they cannot see. The משנה says he meant people the sun 'sees,' meaning people it shines on. Blind people are under the sun like everyone else, so they are included.

phrases.english: MISHNAH: One who vows [not to benefit] from those who see the sun
is forbidden even with the blind,
because this person meant only
those whom the sun sees.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה with a new vow wording.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A vow from 'those who see the sun' includes the blind, since it covers everyone the sun shines on.

steps.title: Why are blind people included?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the reason behind the משנה's ruling.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why the משנה reads the vow this way. This question sets up the explanation that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The plain words 'those who see' sound like they mean people who have sight. So the גמרא wants to know how we can tell that the person meant something wider.

phrases.english: GEMARA: What is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reasoning behind the משנה's ruling.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why does a vow from 'those who see the sun' include blind people?

steps.title: Adding 'the sun' only leaves out fish and fetuses
steps.stepSummary: Because he did not just say 'those who see,' adding 'the sun' only serves to leave out fish and fetuses, which the sun never shines on.
steps.simpleTranslation: Since he did not say 'from those who see.' [The words 'the sun' are there] to exclude fish and fetuses.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the way he worded his vow shows what he meant.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If he had said only 'those who see,' blind people would be left out. Instead he said 'those who see the sun.' That wording points to being under the sun, and it leaves out only creatures the sun never reaches: fish under water and babies not yet born. Blind people are under the sun, so they stay included.
steps.whatToRemember: The exact words a person chooses in a נדר show what he meant. Adding 'the sun' changes the meaning from 'people who can see' to 'people the sun shines on.'

phrases.english: Since he did not say 'from those who see.'
[Saying 'the sun' comes] to exclude fish and fetuses.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 4.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: He chose 'those who see the sun' instead of 'those who see,' so the phrase means everyone the sun shines on. It leaves out only fish and fetuses, so the blind are included.

steps.title: The משנה on vowing from 'the black-headed ones'
steps.stepSummary: A person who vows from 'the black-headed ones' is forbidden from bald and gray-haired men, but permitted from women and children, because only men are called by that name.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: Someone who vows not to benefit from 'the black-headed ones' is forbidden even from bald people and gray-haired people. But he is allowed to benefit from women and children, because only men are called 'black-headed ones.'
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה gives another vow case. It rules that 'black-headed ones' is a name for men, whatever their hair actually looks like.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If we read the words literally, bald and gray-haired men would not count, because their heads are not black. The משנה says they still count, but women and children do not. So the phrase works as a name for a group of people, not as a description of their hair color.

keyTerms.meaning: The black-headed ones, a common name for people

steps.confusionAlert: Do not read 'black-headed' as a test of hair color. The משנה treats it as a name for men, so a bald or white-haired man is still included.

phrases.english: MISHNA: One who vows from 'the black-headed ones'
is forbidden from bald people, and from gray-haired people.
But he is permitted from women and from children,
because only men are called 'black-headed ones.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new vow case in the same series as the earlier cases of seafarers and 'those who see the sun.'
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'Black-headed ones' includes bald and gray-haired men, but excludes women and children.

steps.title: Why are bald people included?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why bald people are included in a vow from 'the black-headed ones.'
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the reason behind the first ruling of the משנה, that bald and gray-haired people are forbidden. It is setting up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The puzzle is simple: a bald man has no black hair at all. So why should a vow about 'black-headed' people include him?

phrases.english: GEMARA: What is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reason behind the רישא of the משנה in step 6.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why bald and gray-haired people are included in 'the black-headed ones.'

steps.title: He did not say 'people with hair'
steps.stepSummary: Because he did not say 'from those with hair,' his words are a general name for people and not a description of their hair.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because he did not say, 'from those who have hair.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question. If he had meant only people with hair, he would have said so.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the same kind of reasoning as step 5. The person chose a set phrase instead of a clear description like 'people with hair.' That shows he was using the common name for people, so bald and gray-haired men are included.

phrases.english: Because he did not say, 'from those with hair.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 7.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Since he did not say 'those with hair,' his phrase is a general name, so bald people are included.

steps.title: Why are women and children excluded?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the second half of the משנה and asks why women and children are not called 'black-headed ones.'
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: But he is permitted from women and children, because only men are called 'black-headed ones.' What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the סיפא of the משנה and asks for its reason. It is setting up the explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Women and children also have black hair. So the question is why the name 'black-headed ones' belongs only to men.

phrases.english: 'But he is permitted from women and from children,
because only men are called black-headed ones.'
What is the reason?

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמוּתָּר בְּנָשִׁים וּבִקְטַנִּים שֶׁאֵין נִקְרָאִין שְׁחוֹרֵי הָרֹאשׁ אֶלָּא אֲנָשִׁים מַאי טַעְמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the רישא of the משנה to its סיפא.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why only men are called 'black-headed ones.'

steps.title: Men's heads are sometimes covered and sometimes uncovered
steps.stepSummary: Men sometimes cover their heads and sometimes uncover them. Women's heads are always covered, and children's heads are always uncovered.
steps.simpleTranslation: Men sometimes cover their heads and sometimes uncover them. But women always keep their heads covered, and children always go with their heads uncovered.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the name fits only men. It points to how each group normally wears their heads.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Men are the group whose heads are sometimes covered and sometimes bare. Women are always covered and children are always bare, so they are a different case. The name 'black-headed ones' is used for the group whose heads go back and forth, which is men.
steps.whatToRemember: In vows, a phrase means what people normally mean by it. 'Black-headed ones' means men, so it includes bald and gray-haired men but not women or children.

phrases.english: Men sometimes have their heads covered
and sometimes have their heads uncovered.
But women are always covered,
and children are always uncovered.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲנָשִׁים זִימְנִין דְּמִיכַּסּוּ רֵישַׁיְיהוּ וְזִימְנִין דְּמִגַּלּוּ רֵישַׁיְיהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 9.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Men's heads are sometimes covered and sometimes uncovered, unlike women (always covered) and children (always uncovered), so the name belongs to men.

steps.title: The משנה on vowing from 'those born' and 'those who will be born'
steps.stepSummary: Someone who vows from ילודים is permitted from נולדים. Someone who vows from נולדים is forbidden even from ילודים.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: Someone who vows not to benefit from 'those who are born' is permitted to benefit from 'those who will be born.' Someone who vows from 'those who will be born' is forbidden even from 'those who are born.'
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה gives two vow phrases about being born. It rules that one phrase is narrow and the other is wide.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ילודים means people already born, so a vow with that word does not cover people born later. נולדים covers more: the vow includes people born later and also people already born.
steps.confusionAlert: The two rulings are not mirror images. ילודים is narrow and leaves out נולדים, but נולדים is wide and includes ילודים too.

phrases.english: MISHNA: One who vows from 'those who are born'
is permitted from 'those who will be born.'
If he vows from 'those who will be born,' he is forbidden from 'those who are born.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new משנה in the same series about the meaning of vow words.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A vow from ילודים does not include נולדים, but a vow from נולדים includes ילודים.

steps.title: רבי מאיר and the חכמים argue about 'those who will be born'
steps.stepSummary: רבי מאיר permits even ילודים in a vow from נולדים. The חכמים say the person meant anyone whose nature is to be born.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי מאיר permits him to benefit even from those already born. The חכמים say: this person only meant 'anyone whose nature is to be born.'
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה brings a מחלוקת about the second ruling, a vow from נולדים. רבי מאיר disagrees, and the חכמים explain why the משנה's ruling on נולדים is right.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר reads נולדים strictly as people born in the future, so people already born are not included. The חכמים say the word means everyone whose nature is to be born, which includes both people already born and people born later.

keyTerms.meaning: Whose nature is to be born

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows the main question behind many vow cases: do we read the exact word, like רבי מאיר, or what the person most likely meant, like the חכמים?

phrases.english: Rabbi Meir permits even those who are born.
phrases.notes: This is about the second case, a vow from נולדים. רבי מאיר says it does not cover people already born.

phrases.english: And the Rabbis say:
This person intended only
anyone whose nature is to be born.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a מחלוקת about the second ruling of step 11.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי מאיר: a vow from נולדים does not include ילודים. חכמים: it means anyone whose nature is to be born, so ילודים are included.

steps.title: If רבי מאיר permits everyone, whom does the vow forbid?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the wording of the משנה. If according to רבי מאיר even ילודים are permitted, and נולדים are surely permitted, then the vow forbids no one.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: According to רבי מאיר, a person who vows from נולדים is permitted even with ילודים, and he is surely permitted with נולדים. But then who is he forbidden from?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reads the word 'even' in רבי מאיר's opinion in the משנה and finds a problem. Read that way, the vow does nothing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says רבי מאיר permits 'even' ילודים in a vow from נולדים. The word 'even' suggests that נולדים are permitted all the more. But a vow that permits both groups forbids nobody, and that cannot be right.

keyTerms.meaning: and it is not even necessary to say
but / rather (here it opens a challenge)

phrases.english: GEMARA:
According to רבי מאיר, [one who vows from those who will be born is permitted even with those already born]
phrases.notes: The bracketed part fills in what רבי מאיר said in the משנה, which the גמרא assumes you remember.

phrases.english: and it is not even necessary to say those who will be born [are permitted].
But then from whom is he forbidden?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the wording of רבי מאיר's opinion quoted in step 12.
steps.kashyaTarget: The word 'even' (אף) in רבי מאיר's statement in the משנה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If 'even' ילודים are permitted, נולדים are surely permitted too, so the vow forbids no one and makes no sense.

steps.title: The משנה is missing words, and here is the full version
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that words are missing from the משנה. רבי מאיר's 'even' is really comparing the case of נולדים to the case of ילודים.
steps.simpleTranslation: Words are missing, and this is what it teaches: one who vows from ילודים is permitted with נולדים. One who vows from נולדים is forbidden with ילודים. רבי מאיר says: even one who vows from נולדים is permitted with ילודים, just as one who vows from ילודים is permitted with נולדים.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא fixes the problem by saying the משנה left words out. It then rewrites the משנה in full.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'even' does not mean 'even ילודים, and surely נולדים.' It means 'even in the vow from נולדים, he is permitted with the other group, just as in the vow from ילודים.' So in each vow רבי מאיר forbids only the exact group the person named, and the vow is not empty.

keyTerms.meaning: it is missing words (the משנה left something out)
and this is what it teaches

steps.confusionAlert: Do not read רבי מאיר's 'even' as 'he is permitted with everyone.' After this answer, 'even' compares the two vows to each other: in each vow he is permitted only with the group he did NOT name.

phrases.english: Words are missing, and this is what it teaches:
One who vows from those already born
is permitted with those who will be born;
[one who vows] from those who will be born
is forbidden [also] with those already born.
רבי מאיר says:
Even one who vows from those who will be born
is permitted with those already born,
just as one who vows from those already born
is permitted with those who will be born.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 13 by rebuilding the text of the משנה.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Missing-words answer (חסורי מיחסרא): adds words to the משנה
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Even' meant רבי מאיר permits both groups, so the vow forbids nobody.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'Even' compares the two vows. In each one, רבי מאיר forbids only the exact group the person named.

steps.title: רב פפא: a פסוק uses נולדים for sons already born
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא challenges the idea that נולדים means 'those who will be born,' since יעקב calls מנשה and אפרים, who were already alive, נולדים.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said to אביי: Are you saying that נולדים means those who will be born? If so, the פסוק says 'your two sons who were born (נולדים) to you in the land of מצרים.' Does that also mean sons who will be born?
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא questions the basic meaning the משנה gives the word נולדים. He brings a פסוק where the word plainly means people already born.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The whole משנה depends on נולדים meaning 'future births.' But in בראשית, יעקב uses נולדים for יוסף's two sons, who were already alive. That shows the word can mean 'already born,' which seems to go against the משנה.

keyTerms.meaning: but if so (opens a challenge from what follows)

phrases.english: רב פפא said to אביי:
Is this to say that "נולדים"
means those who will be born?
But if so,
"Your two sons who were born to you
in the land of מצרים":
does that also mean they will be born?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב פָּפָּא לְאַבָּיֵי לְמֵימְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the משנה's wording to the meaning of the word נולדים itself.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's assumption that נולדים means 'those who will be born.'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A פסוק uses נולדים for sons who were already alive, so the word cannot only mean future births.

steps.title: But another פסוק uses נולד for someone not yet born
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back: if נולדים means 'already born,' then the prophecy about יאשיהו would mean he already existed, which is impossible.
steps.simpleTranslation: But what then, does it mean those already born? If so, the פסוק says 'Behold, a son is born (נולד) to the house of דוד, יאשיהו by name.' Does that also mean he already existed? But מנשה had not even come yet!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers רב פפא by showing the opposite problem. Another פסוק uses the same word for someone who was born only many years later.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If נולד always meant 'already born,' the prophecy about יאשיהו would say he was already alive. But at that time even מנשה, who came generations before יאשיהו, was not yet born. So the word must sometimes mean 'will be born.'

keyTerms.meaning: but rather, what? (you would say the opposite?)

phrases.english: But rather, what? Does it mean those already born?
But if so, that which is written:
"Behold, a son is born to the house of דוד,
יאשיהו by name":
does that also mean he already existed?
But מנשה had not yet come!
phrases.notes: מנשה king of יהודה lived before יאשיהו. If even he wasn't born yet, יאשיהו certainly wasn't.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns רב פפא's challenge around by showing a פסוק that proves the opposite meaning.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea (implied by רב פפא) that נולדים means 'already born.'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The prophecy about יאשיהו uses נולד for someone born generations later, so the word cannot only mean 'already born.'

steps.title: The word means both; for vows, follow everyday speech
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא concludes that נולדים can mean either 'already born' or 'will be born.' In נדרים we follow how ordinary people use the word.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it means this and it means that. And in vows, follow the language of people.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא settles the back-and-forth. The word in the פסוקים can go either way, so for vows we look at everyday speech.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two פסוקים cancel each other out, so the Torah's language cannot decide the question. Instead, a vow is read the way regular people speak. In everyday speech נולדים means those not yet born, which matches the משנה.

keyTerms.meaning: it means this and it means that
follow the language of people (everyday speech)

steps.whatToRemember: A word in a פסוק can have more than one meaning. For נדרים, what counts is how ordinary people talk, not how the word is used in the Torah.
steps.whyThisMatters: The rule 'בנדרים הלך אחר לשון בני אדם' is a basic principle across all of מסכת נדרים for deciding what a vow includes.

phrases.english: Rather, it means this
and it means that,
and in vows,
follow the language of people.
phrases.notes: In everyday speech, נולדים means people not yet born, so the vow is read that way.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the clash between the two פסוקים in steps 15 and 16.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: נולדים can mean either 'already born' or 'will be born.' For vows we follow everyday speech, where it means those not yet born, so the משנה stands.

steps.title: The חכמים say the vow covers only creatures that are born
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the חכמים in the משנה: the person who made the vow meant only creatures whose nature is to be born.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the חכמים say: this person meant only those whose way is to be born.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the next line of the משנה, the opinion of the חכמים. This sets up the question that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The חכמים add a limit to the vow. When someone vows from נולדים, he does not mean every living thing. He means only creatures that come into the world by being born. The גמרא will next ask what this limit leaves out.

keyTerms.meaning: The Sages, the majority opinion in the משנה
Its nature is to be born

phrases.english: And the Sages say:
This one intended only
phrases.notes: 'This one' is the person who made the vow using the word נולדים.

phrases.english: from whoever is the type to be born.

steps.triggerLanguage: וַחֲכָמִים אוֹמְרִים, לֹא נִתְכַּוֵּין זֶה אֶלָּא מִמִּי שֶׁדַּרְכּוֹ לְהִוּוֹלֵד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After finishing the discussion of רבי מאיר's opinion and the meaning of נולדים, the גמרא quotes the חכמים's line from the משנה (step 12) so it can ask what it excludes.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A vow from נולדים covers only creatures whose nature is to be born.

steps.title: What does 'whose nature is to be born' leave out?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what kind of creature the חכמים meant to exclude with this phrase.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does this come to exclude?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what the words of the חכמים leave out of the vow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the חכמים took the trouble to say 'only those whose way is to be born,' there must be some creatures that are not included. The גמרא wants to know which ones.

keyTerms.meaning: To exclude what? What does this leave out?

phrases.english: To exclude what?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about the limit the חכמים just stated.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which creatures are excluded by the words 'whose nature is to be born'.

steps.title: Fish and birds are left out
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the phrase leaves out fish and birds, so the vow does not forbid them.
steps.simpleTranslation: To exclude fish and birds.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that fish and birds are not included in a vow from נולדים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Fish and birds hatch from eggs and are not born from their mother. So in plain speech they are not called נולדים, and a person who vows from נולדים is still allowed to benefit from them.
steps.whatToRemember: According to the חכמים, a vow from נולדים covers only creatures that are actually born. Fish and birds hatch from eggs, so the vow does not include them.
steps.whyThisMatters: This matches the rule from step 17: in נדרים we follow how ordinary people use words, and people do not call hatched creatures 'born.'

phrases.english: To exclude fish and birds.
phrases.notes: These hatch from eggs and are not born from their mother, so the word נולדים does not fit them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 19.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The phrase excludes fish and birds, which hatch from eggs and are not born.
